meta.audience: The people of Noah, then the king and his priests in council
meta.location: The land of Lehi-Nephi; the court of king Noah
meta.date: ~150 BC (Isaiah quoted at v. 21–24, spoken ~700 BC)
principles: Teaching what you do not keep

world_behind.title: Two years, and a disguise
world_behind.text: Abinadi comes back after two years, unrecognized. The record does not say what the disguise was, only that it worked, and it is the reason he gets to finish a sentence before he is seized. A prophet being hunted takes a practical precaution.

world_behind.title: The plague catalogue
world_behind.text: Hail, east wind, insects devouring grain, pestilence, famine. Every item on Abinadi's list is on Egypt's, and he is speaking to a people whose own scripture opens with a deliverance from exactly these. The threat is that they are now on the receiving end.

world_behind.title: "That they might cross him."
world_behind.text: Verse 19 describes cross-examination: questioning designed to trap rather than to learn. A council is convened, a prisoner is produced, and questions are put. What the chapter records is a legal proceeding with a predetermined outcome.

world_behind.title: Isaiah 52 used as a trap
world_behind.text: The priests quote four verses about good tidings, published peace, and a redeemed Jerusalem, and ask what they mean. The quotation is exact against the King James text apart from a single mark of punctuation. Abinadi refuses to answer it here and will answer it in Mosiah 15.

world_behind.title: The Decalogue, opened but not finished
world_behind.text: Verses 34 through 36 give the preface and the first two commandments (I am the Lord thy God, no other gods, no graven image) and then stop. The rest arrives in the next chapter. Abinadi is reciting the law to men who have just claimed to teach it.

world_behind.title: The record explains its own survival again
world_behind.text: Verse 8 says the people will be destroyed but will leave a record, preserved for other nations, "that I may discover the abominations of this people." The reason given for preserving a book is that it testifies against the people who wrote it.

world_behind.title: A plea that forecloses inquiry
world_behind.text: The courtiers do not dispute the prophecy's terms or its source. They assert that no offense exists to be prophesied about. That is the one form of answer that leaves nothing to examine, and the only one no evidence can reach.

words.text: The prophets' word for public mourning: a wail, not a complaint. Abinadi says God will cause them to howl all the day long. The grief is imposed on them. It occurs here once in this record and belongs to Isaiah's vocabulary of ruin.

To trouble persistently. The word appears once in scripture, and its object is a land rather than a person: insects shall pester their land and devour their grain. It is a smaller word than plague and does more damage for being ordinary.

Not to find out. The older sense is to uncover, and the King James prophets use it for pulling the covering off something shameful: Lamentations has God discovering Edom's sins, Micah discovering the foundations of a ruined city. Abinadi's clause runs the same way. A book is kept in existence so that what this people did can be laid open to nations that never met them, which makes the survival of the record a kind of exposure.

A dry one, run over by beasts and trodden. The priests are repeating Abinadi's image back to the king, and the figure they choose is agricultural waste, the part of the plant left after the harvest that nothing wants. They quote it accurately and it does not seem to alarm them.

The promise word, turned around and used as a defense. Lehi's children were told that if they kept the commandments they would prosper in the land, and Benjamin repeated the promise to his own sons at the opening of this book. Noah's courtiers read it backwards: the king has prospered, so the king has not sinned. It is the closest thing to an argument in their whole speech, and the reader has just been shown where the prosperity came from.

To stand against, hold ground. Used twice in one verse of Abinadi under questioning, alongside confound. The priests' astonishment is recorded, so the reader is told that the examination was competent and failed anyway.

phrases.term: Abinadi came among them in disguise, that they knew him not
phrases.text: The practical detail. He had escaped a manhunt at the end of the previous chapter and returned to the same city; the disguise is how. The record notes it without approval or apology, as it notes the guards Zeniff posted.

phrases.term: The life of king Noah shall be valued even as a garment in a hot furnace
phrases.text: A price put on a life, and the unit is cloth in a fire. The image is about worthlessness measured in seconds. The priests will repeat it to the king in verse 10, so the sentence traveled, and it is the one part of the prophecy the court takes personally.

phrases.term: They shall be driven before like a dumb ass
phrases.text: Burdens lashed on their backs, and the animal named is the one proverbially without speech. Mosiah 21 will report the burdens as fact in nearly these words. The humiliation is in the driving.

phrases.term: Yet they shall leave a record behind them
phrases.text: Destruction with an exception attached, and the exception is a book. It is preserved for other nations to read, and the stated purpose is to disclose the abominations of the people who kept it. The record keeps explaining itself, and this is its harshest account.

phrases.term: We have brought a man before thee who has prophesied evil concerning thy people
phrases.text: The charge as filed: prophesying evil. The offense named is the content's unpleasantness, and the accusers report the prophecy accurately in the next three verses without appearing to consider whether it is true.

phrases.term: He pretendeth the Lord hath spoken it
phrases.text: One verb doing all the work of a dismissal. The priests concede that Abinadi said the Lord spoke, and lodge their objection in "pretendeth." Nothing about the message is examined; only the claim to have received it, and that only by insinuation.

phrases.term: We are guiltless, and thou, O king, hast not sinned
phrases.text: Two assertions with no argument attached, followed by a third (this man has lied) and a fourth: we are strong, we shall not come into bondage. The whole defense is a series of denials, and every one of them will be falsified by the next nine chapters.

phrases.term: They began to question him, that they might cross him
phrases.text: The purpose stated with the procedure. They question in order to cross him, so as to have wherewith to accuse. The record is unusually explicit that the hearing was not an inquiry, and unusually explicit that it did not work.

phrases.term: Are you priests, and pretend to teach this people... and yet desire to know of me what these things mean?
phrases.text: Abinadi turns the examination around by refusing the question. The verb he chooses, pretend, is the priests' own from verse 12, and he applies it to their teaching rather than to their belief. Their question exposed them before he answered a word of it.

phrases.term: Ye have not applied your hearts to understanding; therefore, ye have not been wise
phrases.text: Understanding described as something the heart is applied to, like a tool to a task. The failure is one of effort, and the consequence named is unwisdom. The phrase occurs once in scripture.

phrases.term: If ye teach the law of Moses why do ye not keep it?
phrases.text: The question that governs everything Abinadi says for the next three chapters. Four more follow it in the same verse: riches, whoredoms, harlots, causing the people to sin. Each one is a specific charge dressed as a question.

phrases.term: Doth salvation come by the law of Moses? What say ye?
phrases.text: Put to men who have just said they teach that law, and they answer yes. Abinadi's reply does not simply contradict them; it starts reciting the law itself, which turns their answer into the beginning of an examination.

phrases.term: Have ye done all this? I say unto you, Nay, ye have not
phrases.text: He asks and answers both times: have you done it, and have you taught it. The chapter ends on a double refusal delivered by the prisoner, and the men holding him do not reply.

verses.label: v. 1–8
verses.title: The second prophecy
verses.text: He returns disguised after two years and delivers a longer message than the first: fierce anger, bondage, blows, driving, slaughter, bodies left to vultures and dogs; the king's life valued as cloth in a furnace; famine, pestilence, hail, east wind, insects; and a record left behind for other nations to read about them.

verses.label: v. 9–16
verses.title: The arrest and the accusation
verses.text: Bound and carried to the king, charged with prophesying evil. The accusers repeat the prophecy accurately (furnace, dry stalk, thistle blossom), object that he "pretendeth" the Lord spoke, assert their own innocence and the king's, declare they will never come into bondage, and hand him over.

verses.label: v. 17–19
verses.title: The council, and the questioning
verses.text: Prison, a council of priests convened, the prisoner produced, and questions put in order to cross him and find an accusation. He answers boldly, and the record notes that his examiners were astonished.

verses.label: v. 20–24
verses.title: The test question
verses.text: One of them asks what Isaiah 52 means: the feet upon the mountains, the published peace, the watchmen seeing eye to eye, the waste places of Jerusalem singing, the holy arm made bare before all nations. It is four verses of comfort put to a man in chains.

verses.label: v. 25–28
verses.title: The refusal, and the counter-charge
verses.text: Are you priests and pretend to teach, and yet ask me? Wo unto you for perverting the ways of the Lord. Ye have not applied your hearts to understanding. What teach ye this people? And the answer comes back: the law of Moses.

verses.label: v. 29–32
verses.title: Five questions and a claim
verses.text: If you teach it, why do you not keep it? Riches, whoredoms, harlots, and a people led into sin. Then: you shall be smitten; what do you actually know about this law; does salvation come by it? They say yes.

verses.label: v. 33–37
verses.title: The law, begun
verses.text: Abinadi grants that keeping the commandments saves and then starts reciting them: I am the Lord thy God who brought thee out of Egypt, no other God, no graven image. And then the two questions, have you done this and have you taught it, answered both times by the man asking.

chapter.title: The trial is a hearing with the verdict already reached
chapter.text: A council is convened, questions are put in order to produce an accusation, and the record says so outright. What the chapter then documents is the procedure failing. He withstands them all and confounds them, and their astonishment is noted.

chapter.title: The accusers quote the prophecy correctly
chapter.text: Furnace, dry stalk, thistle blossom in the wind: three images repeated to the king with care. They have understood the message and their objection is that it is unpleasant and that the messenger pretends. Nothing in their report suggests they think it might be true.

chapter.title: Four denials, no argument
chapter.text: Verses 14 and 15 assert innocence for the court, innocence for the king, falsehood in the prophet, and immunity from capture. Not one of the four is supported, and every one is refuted by events inside this same book. The record does not need to comment and does not.

chapter.title: Isaiah is used as a weapon and refused as one
chapter.text: The priests pick four verses about good tidings and a redeemed Jerusalem and ask a prisoner to expound them. Abinadi will answer the question three chapters later, on his own terms, after the law has been recited. The delay is the whole point of the exchange.

chapter.title: The charge is teaching what you do not keep
chapter.text: Verse 29 is the hinge of Abinadi's entire ministry: if ye teach the law of Moses why do ye not keep it. Everything from here to his death is an argument about what the law was for and whether men who break it can explain it.

chapter.title: A survival clause with an unflattering purpose
chapter.text: Nephi kept these plates for a wise purpose he did not know; Enos prayed his people's writings would reach their enemies; Mormon said two nations would be judged out of them. Verse 8 adds a fourth answer and it is the harshest: what outlasts this people is the evidence against them.

chapter.title: The prisoner ends the chapter asking the questions
chapter.text: He came in bound and examined; by verse 37 the priests have answered one question wrongly and stopped speaking, and he is putting queries they do not respond to. The reversal happens without any change in who holds the power.

applications.title: Come back after two years
applications.text: The first warning was refused and he returned anyway, with a longer message. If something you said mattered and was rejected, consider whether the right response is distance or another attempt.

applications.title: Notice when you are cross-examining
applications.text: There is a difference between asking to learn and asking to catch. Before your next hard conversation, decide honestly which you are doing.

applications.title: Do not ask what you should already know
applications.text: The priests asked a prisoner to explain a passage they were paid to teach. Identify something you are responsible for understanding and have been quietly outsourcing.

applications.title: Apply your heart to it
applications.text: Understanding is described as effort applied. Take the thing you say you cannot understand and give it the attention you would give a problem at work.

applications.title: Answer the question in verse 29
applications.text: What do you teach, recommend, or insist on that you do not do yourself? Write the specific answer down.

applications.title: Check the guiltless plea
applications.text: "We are guiltless and you have not sinned" is the defense that ends inquiry. When you notice yourself certain there is nothing to examine, treat the certainty itself as the thing to examine.

questions.text: If a record of my life were preserved to be read by strangers, what would it disclose?
Whose message have I dismissed by questioning their motive rather than their content?
What am I sure I am guiltless of, and when did I last actually check?
Do I ask questions to understand people or to corner them?
What have I decided is beyond me that I have simply never worked at?
What do I teach that I do not keep?
